d.title: The accuracy difference has the same cause as the cost difference
d.caption: A bi-encoder must **compress a document into a vector without knowing the query**, so the comparison happens between two summaries. A cross-encoder reads both together and can attend from one to the other — **which is why it is better, and why there is nothing to store.** One fact explains both columns: precomputability and accuracy are the same trade seen from two sides.

d.title: The accuracy you are buying, stated as score separation
d.caption: Both retrievers put `api-idempotency` first, so a ranking metric sees no difference. The difference is in the **spread**: dense ranks 1 to 5 span just **0.3466** (0.6328 down to 0.2863), so **dense genuinely cannot separate those five documents** — its ordering among them is close to arbitrary. The cross-encoder separates them decisively. That is a more useful statement of the benefit than a metric, because it says *why* reranking changes anything.

d.title: Logits, not probabilities — so a score is not comparable across queries
d.caption: The scores range from **−11.457 to +5.905** across the corpus: unbounded, signed, uncalibrated. Which has a consequence people trip on: **a top score of +5.905 on one query and −1.782 on another does not mean the second query failed.** It means the cross-encoder found nothing it liked, and whether that is a failure depends on whether anything relevant exists — so the number is usable for *ordering within a query* and not for thresholding across queries without calibration.

d.title: Three query classes, three different mechanisms failing
d.caption: The baseline fails for **three structurally different reasons**, which is why module 6 needs more than one repair. `Retry-After` returns three documents plausibly about API behaviour and **none containing the header** — the decisive signal is lexical and dense has none. `I forgot my password` works **by luck**, at only 0.3064, because the model happens to bridge *password* and *credential recovery*. And the near-duplicate case gets the right answer first with three near-identical documents behind it.

cells.text: none of the top 3 contains the header

cells: it happens to bridge the words

d.title: A nonsense query scores 0.1279, and a good one scores 0.4630
d.caption: *"What is the airspeed velocity of an unladen swallow"* returns `api-limits` at **0.1279** — a real number, in the same units as the 0.4630 a genuine match earned. So **the scores are not confidences**: there is no value below which the retriever is telling you it found nothing. A threshold can be fitted to one corpus and one query distribution, and it is a fitted constant rather than a property of the score, which 7.1 is about.

d.title: Ranks 5 through 41 are tied at zero, and their order is the sort's accident
d.caption: **Only 4 of 41 documents score above zero** for a two-term query, because most contain neither term. So ranks 5 through 41 are **all tied at 0.0000, and their order is whatever the sort happened to produce** — which matters the moment anything reads beyond the top few: a `fetch_k` of 20 over BM25 returns 4 ranked documents and 16 arbitrary ones, and a fusion step downstream will treat rank 7 as meaningfully better than rank 12.

nodes.label: And fusion will trust those ranks

d.title: Two IDF variants, and one of them can go negative
d.caption: The difference is a `+ 1` inside the logarithm, and it decides whether a score can be negative. **The Lucene-style formula is always positive. `BM25Okapi`'s crosses zero at df = N/2** — so a term appearing in more than half the corpus gets a *negative* weight, meaning a document containing it scores **worse** than one that does not. §04 shows what that does on a small corpus, where df = N/2 is reached easily.

d.title: A term in half the corpus makes the query unanswerable
d.caption: With the term in **1 of 2** documents the Okapi IDF is exactly `log(1.5 / 1.5) = log(1) = 0`, so **both documents score 0.0 and the query is unanswerable.** With it in **2 of 2** the IDF is negative, and the epsilon floor is computed from the average IDF — **which is itself negative here** — so the "floor" is negative too and both documents score below zero. Neither case raises; both produce a ranking with no information in it.

nodes.label: IDF negative, and so is the floor
nodes.sub: the floor is the average IDF

d.title: Both tuning parameters do nothing on this corpus, for stated reasons
d.caption: This is the measurement that stops a pointless sweep. **`k1` does nothing because every matched term appears exactly once** — the term-frequency distribution over all matches is `{1: 13}`, and with `f = 1` the saturation factor multiplies every term in every document by the same amount, so the **order** is unchanged. **`b` does nothing because the documents are the same length**: min 17, mean 25.5, max 39 tokens, standard deviation 4.5. `b` normalises by `|d| / avgdl`, and there is nothing to correct.

d.title: The one failure left after BM25, and no parameter reaches it
d.caption: The worst single case is `I forgot my password`, which scores above zero on **0 of 41 documents.** The relevant document says *"Credential recovery … signed recovery link"* and **contains neither *forgot* nor *password*.** No value of `k1` or `b` reaches that, because **the term is not in the document at all** — which makes it the complement of 6.2's dense failure rather than a weakness of BM25. Dense bridges vocabulary and misses exact terms; BM25 does exactly the reverse, which is the argument for 6.4.

And dense got this one right

d.title: On two queries, the two retrievers share no documents at all
d.caption: `Retry-After`: dense returns `api-idempotency, api-webhooks, bill-refund` and BM25 returns `api-limits, ops-backup, ops-sla` — **no overlap.** `I forgot my password`: dense returns `auth-reset` first and BM25 returns nothing above zero. **They disagree by design**, which is the premise of fusion rather than a problem with it: two retrievers that agreed would be one retriever, and the value of combining them comes entirely from the disagreement.

d.title: Three reasons a weighted sum fails, and the ranges are the first
d.caption: On one query: **dense scores span 0.5757 and BM25 scores span 5.1527** — an order of magnitude apart, so any fixed weight is really a weight times a scale factor nobody wrote down. **Second**, the ranges are per-query: dense's minimum is **negative** here, so a sum can be dragged down by a strongly-disliked document. **Third**, a weight fitted on one query distribution does not transfer, which §04 shows normalisation makes worse rather than better.

d.title: Normalisation destroys the one piece of information that mattered
d.caption: The obvious fix for incomparable ranges is to normalise each retriever's scores to [0, 1], and it is **worse, not better.** On a query where something matched but **nothing relevant did**, normalisation **maps the best irrelevant document to exactly 1.0 — the same value a perfect match would receive.** It destroys the one piece of information that said *this result was weak*, which is the opposite of what a fusion step needs.

d.title: Reading orderings and never scores sidesteps two of the three reasons
d.caption: `EnsembleRetriever` applies reciprocal rank fusion, **reading each retriever's ordering and never its scores.** That sidesteps reasons 1 and 2 entirely: **rank 1 means the same thing whatever scale a retriever's scores are on**, with no normalisation and no per-query calibration. What it does not sidesteps is reason 3 — the weights between retrievers are still a fitted choice, which is what 6.5 measures and finds cannot be fixed by tuning.
